definition: A qualified alternative supplier for the same job. Buyers keep one to win price concessions and to protect supply if the main vendor is short or late; it only works if the second product is good enough to absorb real volume.

A deal that ties shares to a purchase commitment. Either the vendor grants the customer equity (AMD's warrant to OpenAI) or the vendor buys the customer's equity (NVIDIA's OpenAI investment), so supplier and buyer share the upside of the build-out.

The unit AI-infrastructure deals are now sized in: the electrical power drawn by the accelerators, servers and networking (1 GW ≈ several hundred thousand current GPUs). Buyers commit to power because power and sites, not chips, are the binding constraint.

AMD's first rack-scale AI system (2026): 72 Instinct MI455X GPUs, EPYC Venice CPUs and Pensando NICs in a double-wide rack joined by UALink over Ethernet, positioned against NVIDIA's Vera Rubin NVL72.
Shipping a new flagship data-center GPU generation every year instead of every two. It raises the bar for rivals and second sources, which must match a moving target rather than a fixed one.
A condition that must be met before a tranche of a warrant or stock award can be exercised, such as a gigawatt deployed or a share price reached.
